We have carbon NMR data: chemical shifts: 169.52, 132.43,130.27,129.30,126.70,126.66,123.57,43.30,26.29 ppm.

We need number of methyl (CH3) groups in the molecule. Methyl carbons appear around 10-30 ppm for aliphatic, but also 40 ppm for carbon attached to heteroatoms. Here we have peaks at 43.30 and 26.29. Likely methyl groups: 26.29 is typical for CH3 attached to carbon (e.g., isopropyl). 43.30 could be a carbon attached to heteroatom (e.g., carbonyl carbon of acetyl? Actually carbonyl carbon is ~200, not 43). 43 could be a CH2 or CH attached to electronegative atom. Methyl attached to carbonyl (acetyl) appears ~30 ppm. So 26.29 likely methyl. Also maybe 43.30 is a methylene? But we need count of methyl groups. Could be only one methyl.

But we need to be sure. Let's also get proton NMR to see methyl signals.
